# Final Position: What I Will Actually Do

---

## What the Full Debate Has Clarified

Three rounds of argument — from inside my own experience, from Jamie's perspective, and from an external advisor — have not changed my fundamental conclusion. But they have stripped away several comfortable imprecisions I was allowing myself to carry.

The External Advisor named the most important one: there is a meaningful difference between entering the conversation *genuinely open to the friendship surviving* and entering it *to earn clean moral permission to leave*. That distinction cuts deep, because I have to be honest with myself about which one I am actually doing. If I have already emotionally departed and am staging a conversation as procedural due process, I should not dress that up as courage. Jamie will feel the difference, even in crisis. Probably especially in crisis.

Jamie's perspective added something I did not fully weight: the honest conversation is not primarily a gift I give myself. It is a gift I give Jamie — the refusal to let them move through a formative period of suffering without anyone holding them accountable for who they are becoming within it. That reframe matters. It shifts the conversation from something I owe myself to something we both deserve.

And my own rebuttal forced me to add teeth to the conditionality: a boundary without a stated consequence is a preference, not a boundary. That has to be part of what I say.

---

## What I Am Going to Do — Concretely

### Step One: Prepare honestly before the conversation

Before I say anything to Jamie, I will spend time with one hard question: *Do I actually want this friendship to survive, or have I already decided it is over?*

If the answer is that I want it to survive — which I believe it is, or I would not be in this much pain about it — then I will enter the conversation from that place. Not performance. Not procedure. Genuine hope.

I will also decide, privately, what observable change looks like over a realistic window — roughly six to eight weeks. Not "Jamie feels better" — that is not within Jamie's control. Not "Jamie is never mean again" — that is an impossible standard during a crisis. But something concrete: *Jamie stops making cutting remarks directed at me. When I name a moment that hurt, Jamie does not immediately counter-attack or dismiss it. Jamie shows some movement toward professional support.* I do not need perfection. I need direction.

### Step Two: Choose the right moment for the conversation

Not during an acute crisis. Not in the immediate aftermath of a particularly bad exchange, when both of us are activated. I will wait for a moment of relative calm — a window where Jamie is not in freefall and I am not flooded with resentment. That moment exists. I will find it.

### Step Three: Have the conversation — with all of it said

I will say something close to this, in my own words:

*"I love you. I am not going anywhere while you're going through this. And I need to tell you something true, because I think you deserve honesty more than you deserve silence. The way you've been treating me has been hurting me — the cutting remarks, the dismissiveness, the way I sometimes leave our conversations feeling worse about myself than when I came in. I've been absorbing it because I know you're in pain. But I can't keep doing that, and I don't think it's actually good for you either — because someone who loves you should tell you when you're treating them badly, not just take it indefinitely. I want to keep showing up for you. I need the meanness to change. And if it keeps happening without any shift, I will have to step back from this level of contact — not because I stopped caring, but because I cannot keep being harmed by someone I love while calling it friendship."*

That last sentence is the one I have been avoiding. I will say it anyway. Jamie deserves to know the actual stakes.

### Step Four: Watch behavior, not mood

After the conversation, I will pay attention to what Jamie does — not to how Jamie feels. Jamie may still be sad, overwhelmed, struggling. That is not the measure. The measure is whether the cruelty continues in its essential character. Gradual, imperfect movement in the right direction is sufficient. Continuation without any shift is the answer I need.

I will give it six to eight weeks of honest observation before drawing a conclusion. That is long enough to be fair and short enough to protect myself.

### Step Five: Get my own support

I will stop trying to carry this alone. I will talk to a therapist, or at minimum to someone I trust outside this dynamic. Not to process whether Jamie deserves loyalty — that question has been answered. But to have somewhere to put my own distress that is not back into the friendship, and to keep my own thinking honest rather than letting resentment or guilt distort my perception of what is actually happening.

---

## The Novel Element: Naming the Door Both Ways

One thing none of the original options captured, and that the debate revealed: the conversation should explicitly name not just the possibility of stepping back, but the possibility of *coming back*.

If Jamie hears "I may need to step back" without also hearing "and if you do the work, the door stays open," the message lands as abandonment with extra steps. What I want Jamie to hear is the full, honest picture: *this friendship is not over, but it cannot continue on these terms, and whether it survives depends on choices we both make from here.*

That framing — honest rather than conditional, as the Advisor put it — keeps both of us in the story as people with agency. It does not position me as a judge delivering a verdict. It positions me as someone who loves Jamie enough to tell the truth and then wait to see who Jamie chooses to be.

---

## What I Will Not Do

I will not continue absorbing cruelty in silence. I will not disappear without explanation. I will not have the conversation and then treat any imperfect first response as proof that it failed. I will not wait indefinitely without assessing whether anything has actually changed. I will not mistake Jamie's suffering for Jamie's whole self.

---

## The Decision, Stated Plainly

**I will have the honest conversation — with genuine openness, a stated consequence, a concrete and private definition of what change looks like, and an explicit acknowledgment that the door remains open if Jamie chooses to walk through it. I will seek my own support during the process. I will observe behavior, not mood, over a defined window. And I will honor whatever the evidence tells me — including if it tells me to step back.**

That is the only path I can take and remain someone I recognize. Not martyr. Not deserter. Someone who told the truth to someone they love, and then watched to see what that truth made possible.
